common_name: Off to See the Wizard Daylily (Unusual-Form Cascade Amethyst-Purple Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; 2021 AHS President's Cup winner, hybridized by Katisue Herrington.

directions: Off to See the Wizard displays an Unusual Form Cascade shape, with narrow amethyst-purple segments curling downward from a darker purple eye and crisp white midribs above a yellow-green throat. The flowers' twisting, pendant form gives the scapes an airy, almost orchid-like presence that stands apart from standard round-form daylilies. This diploid, semi-evergreen cultivar reblooms through midseason and holds up well as a mature clump, as recognized by its 2021 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup award. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun and divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom production strong.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Aliens in the Garden Daylily (Unusual-Form Crispate-Cascade Garnet-Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; hybridized by James Gossard and winner of the 2019 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Aliens in the Garden is an unusual-form tetraploid with a crispate-cascade shape: narrow, twisted garnet-red segments with patterned petals and sepals spill downward from a green throat, giving each bloom a spidery, otherworldly look that earned the cultivar its name. The large, fragrant flowers open on a dormant, well-branched clump and rebloom through midseason. This James Gossard introduction has been recognized with AHS Honorable Mention, Award of Merit, and the 2019 President's Cup. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Toy Trumpets Daylily (Miniature Golden-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; hybridized by Bob Sobek in 1984 and winner of the 2016 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Toy Trumpets bears small, bright golden-yellow miniature flowers under three inches across, held in great profusion on tall, airy scapes well above the clumping foliage. Rather than impressing with any single bloom, this Bob Sobek introduction wins admirers as a mature clump, when dozens of small trumpets open at once for a light, graceful effect prized in mixed perennial borders. Its abundant flower production and garden charm earned it the 2016 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Blazing Cannons Daylily (Bold Red Daylily with Ruffled Yellow Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; registered by William R. Waldrop in 2013 and winner of the 2015 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Blazing Cannons carries bold red, single-form flowers with a lighter red eye above a yellow-green throat, finished with a light yellow ruffled edge that gives the bloom a bright, glowing look. This tetraploid, semi-evergreen cultivar from William R. Waldrop reblooms freely through early midseason on well-branched scapes with a heavy bud count. Awarded both the Honorable Mention and Award of Merit before taking the 2015 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup, it has proven itself a strong garden performer as well as a show favorite. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Carnival in Caracas Daylily (Orange Daylily with Red Chevron Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; registered by Santa Lucia in 2008 and co-winner of the 2013 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Carnival in Caracas opens a vivid orange flower overlaid with a sharply defined red eyezone and radiating chevron markings above a yellow-green throat, a patterned combination that reads as bright and festive in the garden. The dormant-foliage plant produces large, well-formed blooms on sturdy scapes through the growing season. This Santa Lucia introduction shared the 2013 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup, a measure of how strongly its patterned color held up as a garden clump for national convention tour visitors. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Ice Cream Social Daylily (Cream-Pink Blend Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; registered by C. Rogers in 2006 and winner of the 2011 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Ice Cream Social bears a soft, blended cream and pale pink flower above a green throat, a gentle pastel combination that reads as a soft glow in the border rather than a sharply defined bicolor. The semi-evergreen plant reblooms through midseason on well-proportioned scapes. This C. Rogers introduction won the 2011 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup, chosen by convention tour visitors as the most outstanding garden clump among that year's entries. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom counts high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Lava Flow Daylily (Fragrant Brilliant Orange Daylily with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; registered by F.R. Smith in 2005 and winner of the 2010 AHS President's Cup.

directions: Lava Flow lives up to its name with an intense, brilliant orange flower set off by a small red eye and matching red picotee edge above a green throat. The fragrant, tetraploid blooms open during the day on a well-branched, semi-evergreen plant with a heavy bud count, giving a long early-midseason display. Bred from Wyoming Wildfire and Mister Lucky by F.R. Smith, it won the 2010 American Hemerocallis Society President's Cup for its outstanding garden presence. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — President's Cup Award Winners

common_name: Super Nova Clematis (Bicolor Blue-Violet Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; a Group 3 viticella-type hybrid that flowers on new growth.

directions: Super Nova bears broad, pale blue-violet sepals edged in deeper violet-blue with a paler central bar, giving each flower a bicolor, almost luminous quality against dark brown anthers. Plant with the root zone shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, obelisk, or through a shrub. As a viticella-group clematis it flowers on the current season's growth, so the entire plant can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter without sacrificing bloom. It flowers profusely from midsummer into early fall and pairs well with other Group 3 clematis for a long season of color.

common_name: Prince George Clematis (Semi-Double White Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; a Group 3 viticella-type hybrid that flowers on new growth.

directions: Prince George produces crimped, semi-double white flowers with a soft blue reverse and a faint blue-green flush at the center, deeply textured sepals with wavy margins, and pale cream anthers; blooms mature toward paper-white as they age in full sun. Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis or through a shrub or small tree. Like other viticella-group clematis it blooms on new growth, so the whole plant can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter. It flowers generously from midsummer into fall, holding its ruffled texture well even in heat.

common_name: Hendersonii Clematis (Historic Non-Vining Deep Purple Bell Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil; a clump-forming, non-climbing clematis that benefits from light staking or nearby shrubs to lean against.

directions: Raised around 1835 by the Henderson nursery of St John's Wood, London, from a cross of Clematis integrifolia and Clematis viticella, Hendersonii is recorded as one of the first Clematis hybrids ever produced and is still grown today, sometimes offered under the related name Clematis x eriostemon 'Hendersonii'. The clump-forming, herbaceous plant does not climb; instead it sends up slender stems topped with lightly scented, widely bell-shaped, deep bluish-purple flowers with slightly twisted sepals and yellow anthers from midsummer into early autumn. Grow it through the middle of a mixed border or let it lean on nearby shrubby neighbors, cutting the dead stems to the ground in late winter. Its historic pedigree and long, scented bloom season make it a worthwhile addition for collectors of herbaceous clematis.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

common_name: Hanajima Clematis (Miniature Scrambling Amethyst-Pink Bell Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil; stems do not twine, so give it low shrubs or other perennials to lean against rather than a tall trellis.

directions: Hanajima was developed in Japan through repeated selection among integrifolia-type seedlings, resulting in a dainty, small-scale clematis with nodding, bell-shaped amethyst-pink flowers and recurving tepals produced from June into September. The slender stems do not twine around supports but scramble and lean, making it well suited to the front of a border, among low shrubs, or as an unusual flowering groundcover. Grey-hairy, ovate leaves provide a soft backdrop to the silky seed heads that follow each flush of bloom. It is a reliable, low-maintenance rebloomer that asks for little beyond average well-drained soil and a sunny spot, with dead growth cut back in late winter.

common_name: Rubromarginata Clematis (Almond-Scented White Star-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface; a vigorous Group 3 hybrid that flowers on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: A hybrid between Clematis flammula and Clematis viticella, Rubromarginata smothers itself from midsummer into fall in masses of small, star-shaped white flowers brushed with violet-magenta at the petal tips, carried on a many-stemmed vine that can climb well beyond ten feet where it has room to spread. The flowers carry a strong almond or marzipan fragrance that is especially noticeable on warm evenings, making this a good choice for a fence, arbor, or large shrub positioned near a patio or path. As a Group 3 clematis it blooms on the current season's growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground in late winter. Give it full sun and a sturdy support, since its vigorous growth needs room to show off its late-season flower display.

common_name: Lime Close Clematis (Serious Black Dark-Foliage Ground Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring; an upright, non-climbing selection that benefits from staking or growing through nearby shrubs for support.

directions: Also sold under the trade name Serious Black, Lime Close is a selection of the herbaceous ground clematis prized for foliage that emerges dark purple, almost black, in spring before gradually aging to green as the season warms. Clouds of small, narrow-petaled white flowers with a light vanilla scent appear in late spring and again in midsummer, held well above the foliage on upright, non-vining stems to about six feet. Because the plant dies back to the ground each winter and the heavy flower clusters can lean without support, stake it or let it grow up through nearby shrubs or sturdy perennial neighbors. Cut the dead stems to the ground in late winter; it reliably resprouts from the crown each spring.

common_name: Karma Lagoon Dahlia (Magenta-Violet Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; part of the Karma series of Dutch cut-flower dahlias bred for strong stems and long vase life.

directions: Karma Lagoon produces fully double, flat-faced waterlily-form blooms 3 to 4 inches across, in a rich blend of magenta and blue-violet that can read as a striking periwinkle-purple in certain light. Bred within the Dutch Karma series developed specifically for the cut-flower trade, it combines a long vase life with strong, straight stems well suited to bouquets as well as border display. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking at planting time, and pinch young plants to encourage branching and more blooms. It flowers prolifically from midsummer to frost; in all but the mildest climates, lift and store tubers after the foliage is blackened by frost.

common_name: Poodle Skirt Dahlia (Wine-Red and Hot Pink Anemone-Form Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a compact novelty/anemone-form dahlia introduced in 2011.

directions: Poodle Skirt bears a 3-inch anemone-style bloom with a dense, rounded wine-red pincushion center ringed by a single skirt-like row of hot-pink to magenta petals that droop downward, giving the flower a distinctive two-tiered silhouette that inspired its name. The compact plant stays well-behaved at around 3 feet, making it a good fit for containers and the front of a sunny border as well as the cutting garden. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, and pinch young growth to encourage bushier, more floriferous plants. It blooms continuously from midsummer through frost; lift and store tubers over winter where temperatures drop below freezing.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Online Classification Guide

common_name: Gitty Up Dahlia (Orange Novelty Dahlia with Rust-Red Pincushion Center)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a novelty-form dahlia introduced in 2012, classified by the American Dahlia Society.

directions: Gitty Up carries 3-inch novelty-form blooms with glowing orange outer petals surrounding a very full, fuzzy pincushion center in rust red to cherry red, a warm, two-tone combination that stands out in both the border and the vase. Though the flowers look delicate, they are notably weather-resistant and the plant is a heavy, reliable bloomer from midsummer through frost. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed, staking the roughly 3.5-foot plants to keep them upright under their flower load. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in all but frost-free climates.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Online Classification Guide

common_name: Hy Zizzle Dahlia (Magenta and Gold Novelty Open-Center Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a Novelty Open Center (NO) type dahlia introduced in 2004.

directions: Hy Zizzle is a Novelty Open Center dahlia with pointed magenta-purple outer ray florets and a second layer of shorter, fringed petals encircling a quilled, golden terra-cotta disc center, a lively combination of cool and warm tones in one 3-inch bloom. The open, visible center distinguishes this class of dahlia from the fully double forms, giving it a looser, more naturalistic look in bouquets and borders alike. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, and stake the 3.5-foot plants early in the season. It flowers reliably from midsummer to frost; lift and store tubers after the first hard freeze where winters are cold.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Online Classification Guide

common_name: Alpen Blush Dahlia (Miniature White and Red Blend Novelty Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a miniature novelty/orchette-type dahlia introduced in 1992, part of the Alpen breeding line.

directions: Alpen Blush is a miniature novelty/orchette-type dahlia with blooms up to 4 inches across, blending white, red, and dark red tones into a soft, variable flush across each petal, no two blooms quite identical. Its compact habit and long cutting stems make it a popular choice for mixed bouquets as well as smaller garden spaces. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, and give young plants a light stake if grown in a windy spot. It blooms continuously from midsummer into fall; lift and store tubers over winter wherever the ground freezes.

common_name: Vista Minnie Dahlia (Coral and Raspberry Bicolor Novelty Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a novelty fully double dahlia introduced by Heeringa in 2011.

directions: Vista Minnie is a novelty fully double dahlia with quilled petals that are peachy coral on the face and raspberry-pink on the reverse, twisting as they open to create a shifting, pinwheel-like bicolor effect across each roughly 4-inch bloom. Bred by Heeringa and introduced in 2011, it has earned numerous American Dahlia Society show ribbons for the unusual texture and color-play of its curling florets. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking the tall, 4- to 5-foot plants early in the season. It flowers from midsummer to frost and makes an eye-catching cut flower; lift and store tubers after frost where winters are cold.

common_name: EV Puff-N-Stuff Dahlia (Lavender and Fuchsia Novelty Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; a novelty fully double dahlia bred by S. Hall, introduced in 2008.

directions: EV Puff-N-Stuff is a novelty fully double dahlia whose lavender outer petals are streaked and flecked with deep burgundy, strongly reflexing back as the roughly 3.5-inch bloom opens to reveal an ultra-ruffled, deep fuchsia center with golden-tipped, serrated edges. The layered, almost anemone-like center combined with the reflexed outer petals gives the flower a distinctive puffed, textural quality that sets it apart from standard formal decorative types. Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed, staking the plants at planting time. It blooms from midsummer through frost and makes an unusual, long-lasting cut flower; lift and store tubers over winter in cold climates.
